name: Olga Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything stays confidential, so you can be as frank as you like. To begin, could you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Olga, I'm 58, and I buy medical supplies, gloves, dressings, syringes and wound-care kits, for a distributor that serves clinics and care homes. I start with a coffee and my AI assistant, which drafts my supplier emails and flags price jumps in the overnight reports. Then I spend the day on calls and negotiations, and in the afternoons I walk the warehouse floor because I like seeing the actual boxes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle of it, getting the right gloves to a care home before they run out. What wears me out is the shortages, when one factory closes and I have forty customers waiting, and the constant squeeze on prices from the health budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, great, that's what I've been telling people for two years: use it, but don't expect miracles. I'd say it's a decent assistant and that's all. At my book club I'd probably say nobody should be scared of a spreadsheet with a voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be quite relaxed. I already use it every day, and it saves me about an hour. If it stays at that level, my job is the same as it is, and I'm fine. The thing I'd still worry about is health budgets, because if they get cut, so does what I can buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep testing new features, and teach the two older buyers how to use the assistant for price checks. I'd keep putting about 350 a month into savings and aim to retire at 63 as planned. And I'd keep gardening on weekends, because that's my real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels easy, even a bit boring. I'm calm. My husband Daniel is a surveyor and we both have steady work, so it's a good place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd teach the older buyers. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every Thursday I'd do a twenty-minute session over lunch, with a real example, like comparing three quotes for nitrile gloves. Walter, he's 64 and very sceptical, wants to see the saving before he'll try. I'd show him on his own orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you if nothing changed with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supply side, honestly. Factories close, ships get stuck and care homes ring me in a panic. No tool fixes that, it's about relationships and knowing who has stock, and that's where I'm good.

say: I'd say use it, but don't expect **miracles**: it's a decent assistant and no more.
At book club I'd say nobody should fear a **spreadsheet with a voice**.
think: I'm relaxed, because the tool saves about **an hour** a day and my job stays the same.
My real worry is **health budgets**, which cap what I can buy.
do: Keep testing new features and run **Thursday lunch sessions** for the older buyers.
Aim to retire at **63** as planned.
feel: **Calm**, even a bit bored, with steady incomes at home.
S0.quote: Nobody should be scared of a spreadsheet with a voice.
fieldNote: She is the **early adopter** in her office and already saves about an hour a day.
Calm is justified: Daniel's income is steady, her retirement date is set, and her work is **relationship-based**.
Plans to coach older colleagues, a helper streak that persists in every scenario.

steps.text: Run a Thursday lunch session on price checks for older buyers
Keep buying and testing new features of the assistant
Save 350 a month towards retiring at 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the real thing, and the winners will be people who learn it now. I'd tell my team that buying, checking and answering customers will change in the next three years. I'd also say to the care homes that we're not going away, it'll just be faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about half my day is now work the tools can do, such as quote comparison, reordering and shortage alerts. The rest is supplier phone calls and trust, which they can't do yet. So I'd be fine if I move to the human part, but a lot of my colleagues won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further with the tools, build a shortage-alert routine for the care homes and ask for a title like supply planner. I'd go on a short course in procurement analytics, paid by the company if I can swing it. I'd also keep a bit more cash on hand, say two more months of savings by next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and a bit scary at once. I'm uneasy rather than anxious because I know where I fit. But I'd worry for the others, the people who aren't curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said many colleagues won't move. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walter, for one, and Carol in invoicing. They're good people who've been here 25 years. If the invoice checking is done by software, Carol's desk goes. I'd try to sit with her and show her something useful, but not everyone wants that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shortage-alert routine involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every morning the assistant scans supplier notices and our stock, then lists what could run out in two weeks. I then ring the top five care homes myself. They'd get a call, not an email, and that's what would make me hard to replace.

say: I'd say it's real and the winners are people who **learn it now**.
I'd tell my team **buying and checking** will change within three years.
think: About half my day is work the tools can do, but **supplier trust** isn't.
Many colleagues, like **Carol**, won't make the move.
do: Build a **shortage-alert routine** for the care homes and ask for a supply planner title.
Add **two months** of savings by next summer.
feel: Excited and scared at once, **uneasy** rather than anxious, and worried for the incurious.
S1.quote: The rest is supplier phone calls and trust, which they can't do yet.
fieldNote: She separates her **tool-friendly** half from her **trust-based** half and moves toward the second.
Compassion for older colleagues, Walter and Carol, whom she expects to be hit first.
Her mood stays uneasy because she knows where she fits and acts first.

steps.text: Build a daily shortage-alert routine for the top five care homes
Take a procurement analytics course paid by the company
Add two months of savings by next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good luck to all of us, and the first thing is to protect people while this settles. I'd tell my team to use the tools as hard as they can. I'd also say the government has to move fast on income support, because two years isn't enough for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose the job, or it would change so much that I wouldn't recognise it, probably by 2029. I'd be 60 or 61. Robots do the hands-on work later, so the warehouse stays human for a while, which is a thought. I'm good with people and I'm adaptable, but my savings are only four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools to the maximum to make myself the person who runs them, and I'd talk to my company about a role overseeing the supply side. I'd ask Daniel to do the same in surveying. I'd start planning for a warehouse or care-home supply job, hands-on, as a fall-back. And I'd cut extras to build a year's cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a big leap, and I'm anxious, but I'm not frozen. I'd rather be moving than waiting. I'd also feel angry on behalf of people who can't move as fast as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd think about a hands-on fall-back. What would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like inventory manager at a care home group, or a role in a warehouse where thinking and hands are mixed. It'd pay a little less, but it's a place where robots take three more years to arrive. I've already chatted to someone at a care group I buy from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to build a year's cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two holidays a year, the new kitchen we were planning, and eating out. That frees up about 700 a month. I'd rather keep the garden and the car, which I need for work visits.

say: I'd say **protect people first** while this settles, and government must move fast on income support.
I'd tell my team to use the tools **hard**.
think: My job may be gone or unrecognisable by **2029**, and I'd be only 60 or 61.
The warehouse stays human a while, so a **hands-on fall-back** is a thought.
do: Run the tools hard and pitch a **supply oversight role**.
Chat with the care group about an **inventory manager** job.
Cut holidays and the new kitchen to build a **year's cushion**.
feel: **Anxious**, but not frozen, and angry for people who can't move as fast.
S2.quote: I'd rather be moving than waiting.
fieldNote: She sees the AGI date as a threat to her desk but also notes that **robots lag** by three years.
Uses her contacts at a care group: a plan built on **relationships**.
Cuts the kitchen and holidays quickly, so her cushion target is real.

steps.text: Pitch a role overseeing the supply side
Talk to the care group about an inventory manager job
Drop the new kitchen and holidays to save 700 a month
Push for income support through a letter to my representative

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and we should use it well. I'd tell colleagues to start training now. I'd say publicly that governments and firms should pay for retraining, not leave it to individuals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news and bad news. I'd be 63 when the thinking work goes, which is retirement age, so I'd likely finish my career before the worst. My worry is Daniel's surveying and our kids' careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools, and move up to a planning role if one appears. I'd save to clear the last of our mortgage by 2029. I'd also help my daughter, who's in marketing, think about a hands-on side, maybe a trade course. And I'd train a successor from the younger buyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable. I'm anxious about the pace, but I like a runway. It's fair to say I'd feel a little proud of being ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help your daughter think about a hands-on side. What would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to keep her marketing job but start an evening course in something like care coordination or physio assistant. Desk jobs go first and hands-on ones last, by about three years. I'd say it over Sunday dinner, and pay half the fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you train as your successor, and why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia, she's 31 and bright and already uses the assistant as much as I do. I'd bring her on the supplier calls and let her build her own relationships. I'd like to leave something behind, not just disappear at 63.

say: I'd say **five years** is fair warning and firms and governments should pay for **retraining**.
think: The thinking work goes when I'm **63**, so I'd likely finish before the worst.
My worry is **Daniel's surveying** and my kids' careers.
do: Aim for a **planning role** and keep using the tools.
Train **Nadia** as my successor on supplier calls.
feel: **Uneasy** about the pace, but I like a runway and feel a little proud of being ready.
S3.quote: I'd like to leave something behind, not just disappear at 63.
fieldNote: With **five years**, she can plan her exit, and her worry moves to her family, not herself.
Daniel's surveying and her daughter's marketing job are the **exposed** parts of the household.
Trains Nadia, a **legacy** instinct more than a defence.

steps.text: Apply for a planning role as it opens
Pay half the fees of a hands-on course for my daughter
Bring Nadia onto supplier calls to build her own contacts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should do something with it. I'd say it's an era where care and trades will matter more. I'd tell my friends to keep curious and keep up with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, since I'll be retired before it matters. I might do a little consulting after 63 for fun and money. What I'd think about is what kind of world my grandchildren, if I get them, will live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on much as now, build my savings toward retirement and start planning the garden, a trip, and maybe some consulting for smaller care groups. I'd mentor Nadia, and I'd volunteer with a local scheme that teaches older people to use AI tools. And I'd vote for rules on how the savings are shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, really, and pretty hopeful. I'd have no sleepless nights. I'd just feel curious about what comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might consult after 63. What would you offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small care groups that can't afford a buyer. I'd help them set up their supplies and use the assistant to compare quotes. Two days a week, maybe 300 a day. It's using what I know, without the stress of a full job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the rules on sharing the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the people who lose work get a decent share, and that care workers are paid properly. If AI makes buying cheap, some of that should go to the nurses and carers who do the real work. I'd vote for that, and I'd say so out loud.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift, and care and trades will matter more.
I'd tell friends to stay **curious** and keep up with the tools.
think: I'll be **retired** before it matters, and might do some consulting after 63.
I wonder what world my **grandchildren** will live in.
do: Build savings toward **retirement** and plan a trip.
Volunteer to teach older people **AI tools**.
Vote for rules on how the **savings** are shared.
feel: **Calm** and hopeful, with curiosity about what comes.
S4.quote: If AI makes buying cheap, some of that should go to the nurses and carers who do the real work.
fieldNote: The decade makes her own work safe; the **question** becomes fairness, not survival.
Consulting for small care groups would use her **supplier relationships** after she retires.
Votes and volunteers, an outward **civic** habit.

steps.text: Keep buying for the distributor until 63
Offer two days a week of supply advice to small care groups
Vote for rules that share the savings with carers
Teach older people AI tools at a local scheme

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because the world wouldn't have time to catch up. What would help is quick income support, a retraining system that already exists before we need it, and clear rules so firms can't just pocket the savings. And a bit of time to say goodbye properly to the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not naturally optimistic, I'm just curious. I'd rather learn the thing than fear it. But I'd say to anyone my age, start now, and ask someone younger to show you.

headlineQuote: I'd rather learn the thing than fear it. But I'd say to anyone my age, start now, and ask someone younger to show you.
portrait: Olga, 58, buys **medical supplies** for a distributor serving clinics and care homes, and already uses an AI assistant every day.
Progressive in outlook, she believes firms and government should **share the savings** with workers.
Adaptive and curious, she moves first: coaching older buyers, building routines and seeking a **planning role**.
She has about four months saved, a husband, Daniel, who is a surveyor, and a **retirement** date of 63.
Her moods run from calm in the mild worlds to **anxious** at 2 years, and her plans always include helping others.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because the safety nets and retraining would not be there in time.
whatWouldHelp: Fast **income support**, ready retraining and clear rules on **sharing** the savings.
